summary: Describes the Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+) protocol, widely used to provide device administration for routers, network access servers and other equipment through centralized servers. It documents the protocol as deployed and is informational.

eli5.summary: Network equipment needs to know who may log in and what they may do. TACACS+ lets a central server make those decisions for many devices. This document writes down how that protocol works.

questions: how does tacacs+ authenticate device administrators
subtitle: How network devices ask a central server who may log in, what they may do, and what they did.

tldr.problem: Routers, network access servers and similar devices need a central place to decide who may administer them, what each person may do, and a record of what was done. The protocol deployed for this was only ever written down in an unstandardized draft.
tldr.mechanism: TACACS+ runs over TCP and splits the job into three separate exchanges, authentication, authorization and accounting, each with its own packet types behind a common 12-byte header. The body is obfuscated with an MD5-based pad and a shared secret.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8907 documents the Device Administration subset of the old draft, removes SENDPASS, deprecates redirection, and says plainly that the obfuscation is not real encryption, so TACACS+ must run on a secured, separated network. It has been updated by RFC 9887.

today: RFC 8907 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 9887, which specifies securing the TACACS+ connection with TLS 1.3. It documents the protocol as already deployed rather than defining a new Internet Standard.

sections.title: What TACACS+ Is For
sections.content:
TACACS+ was conceived as a general Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) protocol, but it is mainly used for Device Administration: authenticating access to network devices, centrally authorizing operations, and auditing them. The protocol was defined in a document that was never standardized, known as 'The Draft'. This RFC is informational and clarifies the subset of the draft common to Device Administration implementations.

Three things were taken out or changed: SENDPASS is removed for security reasons, the normative description of legacy features such as ARAP and outbound authentication is dropped, and forwarding to an alternative daemon (TAC_PLUS_AUTHEN_STATUS_FOLLOW) is deprecated. The separation of authentication, authorization and accounting is a key design element, and a deployment need not use all three.
sections.eli5: Network gear needs a boss who says who may sign in and what they may touch. This document writes down how that boss and the gear talk, and drops a few risky old tricks.

sections.title: Packets, Connections and Obfuscation
sections.content:
Every packet starts with a 12-byte header holding the version, packet type (authentication, authorization or accounting), a sequence number, flags, a session_id and the body length. TACACS+ uses TCP, and server port 49 is allocated by IANA. A session is one authentication sequence, one authorization exchange or one accounting exchange. Clients send odd sequence numbers and servers send even ones, starting at 1.

With Single Connection Mode, set by a header flag in the first two packets, a client can multiplex several sessions on one TCP connection. The server may refuse it or close the connection after a period of inactivity.

The packet body is obfuscated by XOR with a pad built from chained MD5 hashes of the session id, the shared secret key, the version and the sequence number. The RFC avoids calling this encryption because the algorithm would not meet modern standards. A flag can turn obfuscation off, but it MUST NOT be used in production and a request with it set MUST be dropped.
sections.eli5: Every message has a label on the outside saying what kind it is, which conversation it belongs to and how long it is. The inside is scrambled with a secret both sides know, but the scrambling is weak, like a simple code ring.

sections.title: Authentication
sections.content:
Authentication works as a START packet from the client followed by REPLY packets from the server. If the server needs more, it replies with GETUSER, GETPASS or GETDATA, and the client answers with a CONTINUE. The server ends the session with PASS, FAIL or ERROR. If it sets the NOECHO flag, the client MUST NOT show the answer as it is typed.

The authen_type field selects ASCII, PAP, CHAP, MS-CHAP version 1 or MS-CHAP version 2. ASCII login can take several rounds, and the server MUST limit retries for a missing username, with three recommended. PAP, CHAP and MS-CHAP logins are a single START and a single REPLY and use minor version 1. An ENABLE request changes the privilege level, comparable to Unix su.

A client may abort with the abort flag in a CONTINUE. RESTART asks the client to start over with a new session id, possibly with a different authentication type. A client should treat FOLLOW as FAIL.
sections.eli5: Signing in is a short chat. The device says 'someone wants in', the desk asks 'who are you?', then 'what is your password?', and finally says yes or no.

sections.title: Authorization, Accounting and Privilege Levels
sections.content:
Authorization decides what a user may do. It is always one pair of messages: a REQUEST from the client and a REPLY from the server. Requests carry argument-value pairs, where an equals sign separates a mandatory argument from its value and an asterisk an optional one. A server answers PASS_ADD (apply the response arguments in addition), PASS_REPL (use them instead), FAIL or ERROR. A client that gets a mandatory argument it cannot handle MUST treat the authorization as failed. Common arguments include service, cmd, cmd-arg and priv-lvl.

Accounting records events with start, stop and watchdog flags, so a server can keep an audit trail or billing data. START and STOP are mutually exclusive, and the server MUST reply with success only when the record has been recorded. For Device Administration, clients MUST send an accounting start packet for every command entered.

Privilege levels run from 0 to 15, each a superset of the next lower, and are mapped by the client to permitted actions. Support is not mandatory for clients but SHOULD be provided by servers.
sections.eli5: After you are in, the device asks the desk what you may do, like 'may this person change settings?'. It also writes down what you did, like a visitor logbook. Higher levels get more keys.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Best Practices
sections.content:
The RFC is blunt: the protocol has no security mechanism that meets modern requirements. The obfuscation provides no meaningful integrity, privacy or replay protection, so an attacker with access to the data stream should be assumed able to read and modify all packets. Known weaknesses include brute-force attacks helped by MD5, known and chosen plaintext attacks, and no forward secrecy. CHAP does not protect the username from a trivial man-in-the-middle attack.

Operators therefore MUST NOT rely on the obfuscation, and TACACS+ MUST be deployed on networks that ensure privacy and integrity and are separated from other traffic. New implementations MUST follow these practices:

  • Servers allow a unique secret per client, support keys of at least 32 characters, and accept connections only from known clients.
  • Servers reject the unencrypted flag, and clients MUST NOT set it.
  • Servers can be set to accept only challenge/response types (CHAP, MS-CHAP).
  • The redirection mechanism is deprecated and, if implemented, is disabled by default.
sections.eli5: The secret code used here is easy to crack, so you must keep the whole channel private, like talking in a locked room, instead of trusting the code.

fields.name: Sequence number
fields.desc: Starts at 1; clients odd, servers even.

fields.name: Session ID
fields.desc: Constant for the session; MUST come from a cryptographically strong random generator.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the packet body, not including the header.
